cue: Hold the phone close to the ground and turn it slowly. A woodlouse heads for the darker side.

src: docs/views/sheets/crab.md#2 All around: Zeil and Hemmi 2006; Zeil and Al-Mutairi 1996
fov.note: the sources give a panoramic field and no number; the engine compresses it to half scale

src: docs/views/sheets/crab.md#2 Sharpness: Zeil and Al-Mutairi 1996 (0.39 cycles per degree, Uca lactea annulipes)
cpd.note: measured in one fiddler crab and drawn for every decapod

src: docs/views/sheets/crab.md#2 Colour: Bruno, Mote and Goldsmith 1973; Jordao, Cronin and Oliveira 2007
M.note: one main pigment near 500 nm, so reds go dark; the engine's two-cone model stands in and is the app's choice

sheen.note: a violet sheen for the ultraviolet a phone cannot record; the strength is the app's

src: docs/views/sheets/crab.md#2 Pace: Brodrick, How and Hemmi 2022 (73.6 Hz, light-adapted by day)
rate.note: 60 over 73.6 is 0.82; a crayfish's movement fibres follow only about 10 Hz and were not used

field.note: inferred from facet counts; no resolution is measured in a woodlouse

crab_protan.note: Vienot, Brettel and Mollon 1999, as in the squirrel view; entered from memory

shadow.note: how dark the ring is when the light falls

overlay.name: shadow
overlay.note: when the light falls suddenly, a dark ring runs out from where it fell (atlas 14); woodlice turn toward dark shelter

rows: Two small-eyed water isopods have 4 and about 25 facets to an eye, and a close picture of a Rough Woodlouse’s eye shows 22. The Asian shore crab has 2,400 to 6,000.
The sea slater, a big-eyed seashore relative, has facets about 7 degrees apart, which resolves about 0.07 cycles per degree, near an eight-hundredth of your 60.
With about twenty facets to an eye, a woodlouse is drawn with no image at all, only how much light there is and from where.
Woodlice turn away from light toward dark shelters, where the air is damper and cooler.
Woodlice shelter more when the air is dry, and huddled together they lose about half as much water as they do alone.
About six in ten Common Pill Woodlice are active at night, against nine in ten of Philoscia muscorum, the fourth most recorded woodlouse.
No measurement of a woodlouse’s colour sense was found, so the picture is grey.
How far and how evenly a woodlouse walks changes with the dampness of the air, which a camera cannot show.
With &draw=shadow, a sudden fall of light sends a dark ring across the picture. The ring is the app's drawing.
